title: Internal Bridges
titleHtml: Build bridges before you need them.
tagline: Networking without the ick: building internal bridges.
description: A 45-minute virtual session for all Vanderbilt staff: connect across departments with genuine curiosity, run the 20-minute virtual coffee, and keep your bridges warm with small, real follow-ups.
heroLead: If networking makes you cringe, you have seen it done badly. This session rebuilds it on genuine curiosity, packed into a 20-minute coffee you would actually take.
objectives: Swap transactional networking for curiosity-based connecting across departments
Run a 20-minute virtual coffee, from the invite to the thank-you
Keep a bridge warm with small, genuine follow-ups that take two minutes
missionTie: Radical Collaboration is a chancellor-level bet that Vanderbilt's best work happens across boundaries, and every bridge between departments is that bet paying off at human scale.

agenda.d: Curiosity is the whole trick: real questions beat working a room.
The invite, the questions, and the close of a coffee worth taking.
Two-minute follow-ups that keep a connection alive for years.

manifesto: Curiosity builds the bridge; small follow-ups keep it standing.

sections.headline: Curiosity is the whole trick.
sections.lead: The ick comes from networking as extraction: collecting contacts you plan to use someday. Curiosity flips it. You reach out because you genuinely wonder how enrollment forecasts get made, or what facilities sees at 5am. Genuine interest carries no ick.
sections.group: In pairs: name one Vanderbilt team whose work you are genuinely curious about, and the question you would ask them. 90 seconds each.
sections.solo: Name one Vanderbilt team you are genuinely curious about, and the question you would ask them.

card.text: Before reaching out, find the question you actually want answered about their work. If you have one, the outreach will feel natural to send and to receive. If you cannot find one, you picked the wrong person, and no script will fix it.

interaction.q: What separates connecting from the networking that feels gross?

opts.why: Frequency was never the problem. One extraction attempt feels worse than a dozen genuinely curious conversations.

opts.t: Leading with a question you genuinely want answered
opts.why: Exactly. Curiosity makes the outreach honest, gives the conversation a spine, and leaves both people better off whether or not anything comes of it.

opts.t: Only connecting with people at your own level
opts.why: Curiosity travels in every direction. Some of the best bridges run to people whose work looks nothing like yours; that distance is the value.

interaction.context: The ick is worth trusting: it is what extraction feels like from the outside. Curiosity is the honest replacement, and last month primed it. Seeing the talent around you means you already know whose work makes you wonder, and a real question is the only script this ever needs.
interaction.discuss: When has an outreach felt gross to receive, and what gave it away? What would the genuinely curious version of that same message have sounded like?

deeper.title: When the curiosity will not come
deeper.body: Curiosity can be primed. Skim the university news page, reread your department's last newsletter, or chase the last process that mystified you: who decides that, and how do they know? The question you want survives a simple test: you would still ask it if nothing ever came of the coffee. If a person interests you only for their influence, the test failed; start from the work you wonder about.
steps: Write down three Vanderbilt processes that genuinely mystify you, and the team that owns each one.
For one of them, draft the question you would ask even if the coffee never led anywhere else.

sections.headline: Twenty minutes, well spent.
sections.lead: The 20-minute virtual coffee is the unit of internal networking: short enough to say yes to, long enough to matter. The invite decides whether it happens; the questions decide whether it was worth it. Build both.

interaction.intro: You are inviting someone from another department to a 20-minute virtual coffee. Choose the invite and the twenty minutes.

opts.t: Hi! I'd love to pick your brain sometime. Coffee?
opts.coach: Vague ask, unbounded time, no reason. 'Pick your brain' tells them the meeting is work for them and a favor to you. Easy to ignore.

opts.t: I'm trying to grow my network at Vanderbilt. Could we meet?
opts.coach: Honest, and it makes the coffee about your goals. The reason to say yes needs to include them, or at least their work.

opts.t: I saw your team rebuilt orientation. I'm curious how you pulled it off. 20 minutes sometime?
opts.coach: Specific, flattering because it is true, and bounded at 20 minutes. You gave them a reason that is about their work. This one gets a yes.

opts.t: Walk through your background and mention you are open to opportunities.
opts.coach: That turns a coffee into an audition nobody scheduled. The fastest way to make an internal contact go cold is to make them your job lead.

opts.t: Keep it loose and see where the conversation goes.
opts.coach: Pleasant, and it drifts. Without a couple of real questions the twenty minutes evaporates and neither of you can say what it was for.

opts.t: Ask your three real questions, listen hard, and end at twenty with a thank-you.
opts.coach: Questions carry the meeting, listening makes you memorable, and ending on time is what earns the second yes.

heads.strong: A coffee they would take again. You left with real insight and they left feeling interesting, which is rarer.
heads.mid: Pleasant and shapeless. Nobody regrets it; nobody remembers it either.
heads.weak: They saw the ask coming and went politely vague. The bridge is now harder to build than before you started.

reactions.strong: Three weeks later they forward you a posting on their team with 'thought of you.' You did nothing but be curious and end on time. That is how bridges start carrying traffic.
reactions.mid: A month later neither of you could say what the coffee was about. The next invite starts from scratch.
reactions.weak: Your name now arrives with a small flinch attached. When a role opens on their team, they remember the audition, and they think of someone else for it.

deeper.title: Three questions that carry the meeting
deeper.body: The best coffee questions share a shape: they ask how the work happens. 'What surprised you about the orientation rebuild?' opens stories; 'any openings coming up?' closes them. Prepare three in advance, then let the second and third bend toward whatever the first answer surprised you with. Prepared and rigid are different things, and the bend is where the conversation gets good.
steps: Draft the three questions for the coffee on your capstone card. Test each one: is it about their work?
Plan the close: the thank-you plus the one specific detail you want to remember from their answers.

sections.headline: Small follow-ups, long bridges.
sections.lead: A bridge left untouched goes quiet, though the dormant-ties research has good news: reconnected contacts often bring fresher insight than current ones, and the trust survives the silence. The two-minute follow-up keeps you from needing that rescue. Read each one and call it.

source.label: Dormant ties research, Levin, Walter, and Murnighan (MIT Sloan Management Review)

sections.group: In pairs: name one contact in another department you could send a two-minute warm follow-up to this week. What would it say?
sections.solo: Name one contact in another department and the two-minute warm follow-up you could send this week.

interaction.intro: Warm, transactional, or too much? Read each move and call it.
interaction.passMsg: You have the touch: specific, generous, occasional. Bridges kept that way hold for years.
interaction.failMsg: Close. The tell: warm follow-ups are specific and ask for nothing. Asks after long silence read as extraction, and daily contact reads as pressure.

items.q: A month after your coffee, you spot an article on the system they said they were migrating to. You send the link with one line.
items.why: Two minutes, specific to them, asks for nothing. This is the perfect warm follow-up: proof you listened, delivered with no invoice attached.

items.q: You have not spoken in months. A role opens on their team. Your first message is your resume and 'any chance of a referral?'
items.why: Cold silence, then an ask: the extraction pattern that gave networking its ick. Warm the bridge first, or make the ask plainly without presuming a relationship.

items.q: Tuesday's coffee went great. You sent a thank-you Wednesday, a LinkedIn request Thursday, and are drafting a Friday check-in.
items.why: The thank-you was perfect; the rest is crowding. Bridges are kept warm monthly, with moments that matter, and never by volume.

deeper.title: A cadence you will actually keep
deeper.body: The follow-up habit dies when it turns into homework. Attach it to moments instead of a schedule: you read something and think of them, their team ships something visible, a conversation echoes a thing they told you. Two minutes at the moment of thinking beats any reminder to be thoughtful later. A handful of bridges kept this way carries more opportunity than a hundred contacts kept cold.
steps: List the internal contacts you would call bridges today, and note when each one last heard from you.
Pick the coldest bridge still worth keeping and send its two-minute reopener before you close this tab.

recap.q: What takes the ick out of internal networking?
opts: Doing it only at official events
Leading with genuine curiosity about their work
Keeping every coffee under ten minutes
recap.why: Curiosity makes outreach honest. If you have a question you truly want answered, the connection carries itself.

recap.q: What makes a virtual-coffee invite easy to say yes to?
opts: Keeping it vague so they can shape it
Offering to buy them an actual coffee
A specific reason about their work, capped at 20 minutes
recap.why: Specific plus bounded gets the yes. 'Pick your brain sometime' is vague, unbounded, and all about you.

recap.q: A month after a good coffee, the best bridge-warming move is...
opts: A resume, in case something opens
A specific two-minute follow-up that asks for nothing
A daily stream of likes and comments
Waiting for them to reach out first
recap.why: Specific and generous keeps the bridge warm. Extraction asks and radio silence both let it quietly fall down.

recapMsgs.high: The bridge kit is complete. Now pick your first coffee.
recapMsgs.mid: Solid. Revisit the section you missed, then build your card.
recapMsgs.low: Worth a second pass through the three sections before you commit.

capstone.headline: One bridge, started this week.
capstone.lead: Pick the bridge move you will actually make. Teams and roles, never names; nothing you type is saved or sent.
capstone.whoLabel: Where does the bridge go? A team or role, and your genuine question.
capstone.whoPlaceholder: e.g. analyst on the enrollment team; how do the fall forecasts get made?
capstone.practiceLabel: Which bridge move do you make?

practices.name: The curiosity coffee
practices.move: Send one specific, bounded invite to someone in another department: their work, your genuine question, 20 minutes.

practices.name: The warm follow-up
practices.move: Send one two-minute follow-up to a contact you already have: a link, a congratulations, or a thank-you with a specific detail.

practices.name: The bridge map
practices.move: List three teams your work touches but you have never met, and the one person you would ask for a coffee in each.

whens.out: The move happens today, before you close this tab.
The move happens this week, sent by Friday.
The move happens within two weeks, booked today so it cannot slide.

capstone.evidenceRow: Afterward, one line: what did you learn about their work that you could never have guessed?

closing.headline: Build the bridge before you need it.
closing.lead: You rebuilt networking on curiosity, packed it into twenty minutes, and learned the two-minute follow-up. With Monday's sending managers and Tuesday's Portal walkthrough, the month's whole map is in your hands.
closing.nextTag: Your one next step · This week
closing.nextTitle: Make the bridge move on your card
closing.nextBody: Send the invite or the follow-up exactly as built. If growing a team is your next stretch, this month's LinkedIn Learning pick is Building Your Team by Chris Croft.

facilitator.audience: All Vanderbilt staff in the Anchor's Edge weekly rhythm; no management experience assumed. Works for 6 to 40 on a call; breakouts run in pairs. No prerequisites; November is the Transfer Portal in Practice month, and this session builds its human network.
facilitator.pulse: Seven days out, send the pulse: 'Did the bridge move on your card happen? What did you learn that you could never have guessed? Which bridge is next?' Count of sent invites and follow-ups is the Level 3 metric for the month.

s1.title: Networking without the ick
s1.say: Let's name it: for most people, the word networking triggers a small full-body cringe. Good. The cringe is accurate; it is what extraction feels like from the outside. Today we throw that version out. The replacement runs on one fuel: genuine curiosity about how other people's work actually happens. You will never need a script again, because a real question is the script.
facilitate: Read the curiosity test card aloud once.
Show the in-the-room card in place of the quiz; ask in chat for one word on what makes networking feel gross.
Open the discussion: an outreach that felt gross to receive, and its curious version. Two or three voices.
Run the breakout: one team you are curious about and the question you would ask.

ask.q: Which Vanderbilt team's work are you genuinely curious about?
expect: Often a team they collaborate with but have never really met
Sometimes something completely unrelated to their role
ask.respond: Notice how easy that question was. That is the whole reframe: your curiosity already exists; networking is just letting it out of the building.

s1.debrief: The curiosity test does the filtering: a real question means the right person, and no question means the wrong one.
s1.watchFor: Self-identified introverts opting out early. Name it: this model favors them; one genuine question beats an hour of working a room.
s1.transition: Curiosity needs a container. Ours is twenty minutes long.
s1.coreNote: Core: skip the breakout; run the context card and take three curiosity targets in chat.

s2.title: The 20-minute coffee
s2.purpose: Give everyone a repeatable format: the specific bounded invite and the question-led twenty minutes.
s2.say: The unit of internal networking is the 20-minute virtual coffee. Twenty minutes is short enough that a stranger says yes and long enough to actually learn something. But the coffee is won or lost in the invite: specific about their work, honest about your curiosity, and bounded in time. Then the twenty minutes themselves: your questions, their answers, your full attention, and a clean ending.
facilitate: Run Build the coffee; two minutes to choose both slots and run it.
Ask one volunteer to read their outcome aloud, weak or strong.
Point at the pattern: specific bounded invite, question-led minutes.

ask.q: Why does ending at twenty minutes matter so much?
expect: It proves you meant the invite
ask.respond: All three, and it compounds: the person who ends on time is the person whose next invite gets accepted within the hour.

s2.debrief: Specific invite, real questions, clean ending. The format is small on purpose; small is what makes it repeatable.
s2.watchFor: People drafting invites that are secretly job inquiries. Redirect to the curiosity test: the coffee is for learning, and opportunity follows on its own.
s2.transition: One good coffee is a plank. Keeping it warm is what makes it a bridge.
s2.coreNote: Core: everyone runs the builder solo; skip the read-aloud.

s3.title: Keeping bridges warm
s3.purpose: Install the two-minute warm follow-up habit and the instincts for cadence.
s3.say: Here is where most bridges die: the coffee goes great, everyone means to stay in touch, and eleven months later the connection is too cold to use. The fix costs two minutes: a link about something they mentioned, a congratulations on their project, a thank-you with one specific detail. Specific, generous, occasional. That cadence keeps a bridge warm for years, and it is the difference between a contact list and a network.
facilitate: Run Call the follow-up live; everyone plays on their own screen.
After round two, pause on the resume-after-silence pattern; ask why it lands so badly.
Run the breakout: one contact and the two-minute follow-up you could send.

ask.q: What makes the article-link follow-up in round one so effective?
ask.respond: Right. Generosity at two-minute scale is the most underpriced move in professional life. Nobody forgets the person who remembered.

s3.debrief: Warm follow-ups are specific, generous, and occasional. The bridge you keep warm is the one that carries opportunity later.
s3.watchFor: People turning the follow-up into a scheduled campaign. Keep it human: when you genuinely think of them, send the two minutes.
s3.transition: Quick recap, then you pick your first bridge.
s3.coreNote: Core: run the trainer, skip the breakout, take one voice on the debrief question.

facilitator.capstoneSay: Now make it real. One bridge: a team, your genuine question, and the move you will make. Teams and roles, never names. Build the card and copy it somewhere you will see it before Friday. Two minutes, quiet, go.
facilitator.closeSay: You leave with a curiosity test, a coffee format, and a two-minute habit. That closes the Transfer Portal week: Monday gave managers the sending mindset, Tuesday walked the Portal end to end, and today built the bridges that carry the news. If you want more this month, the navigators are running a live Portal walkthrough and a skill-profile clinic, and the LinkedIn Learning pick is Building Your Team by Chris Croft. Next month the series takes up the Vanderbilt Manager Standard; same time, same rhythm.

contingencies.if: Screen share or the site fails mid-session
contingencies.then: Paste the learner link in chat and narrate from your own browser; every interaction runs on learner devices without the share.
Run the breakout prompts as 60-second chat storms: everyone types their answer at once, you read the best three aloud.

contingencies.if: Someone says they have no time for networking
contingencies.then: Do the math aloud: one 20-minute coffee and two 2-minute follow-ups a month is under half an hour. Compare that with the cost of starting every search, project, and question from cold.

contingencies.if: A participant wants to network only for a specific job they are chasing
contingencies.then: Honor the goal and widen the frame: a live application is Portal work, and a navigator can help today. Bridges are the long game that means the next opportunity finds them.

toughQuestions.q: Isn't this just politics with better branding?
toughQuestions.a: Politics is managing impressions; this is trading genuine curiosity. The test is simple: if the other person got nothing from the exchange, it was politics. A good coffee leaves them feeling interesting and you knowing more. Both sides gained.

toughQuestions.q: I'm an introvert. Is there a version of this for me?
toughQuestions.a: This is the introvert version: one person, twenty minutes, prepared questions, and listening as the main event. The model that requires working a room is the one we threw out in section one.

toughQuestions.q: What if I invite someone senior and they ignore me?
toughQuestions.a: Expect some silence; senior calendars eat invites. A specific, bounded, curious invite lands better than you fear, and one gentle nudge after two weeks is fine. After that, pick another door; curiosity has plenty of targets.

templates.title: Pre-work invite (paste into the calendar invite)
templates.body: Subject: Thursday, 45 minutes on networking without the ick. Bring one team at Vanderbilt you are genuinely curious about. That is the only homework. Live and interactive; have the session link open on your own screen.

templates.title: 7-day pulse (send one week after)
templates.body: Subject: Did the bridge move happen? Three lines, reply whenever: 1) Did the invite or follow-up on your card go out? 2) What did you learn that you could never have guessed? 3) Which bridge is next?
